claims.claim_vi: The source defines a distributed lock as a mechanism ensuring mutual exclusion across a distributed system and lists six use cases: leader election, task scheduling, resource allocation, microservices coordination, inventory management, session management, with a one-or-two-sentence gloss each.
claims.verified_by: Source body read at the pinned commit.

claims.claim_vi: Toy run: client A acquires a lock at step 0 with TTL 10 and pauses until step 15; B acquires it at step 12 and writes; A then writes. Without a fencing check the store accepts both writes and ends with A's value; with a store that rejects tokens lower than the highest seen, B's write (token 2) is accepted and A's (token 1) is rejected.
claims.verified_by: Run by the author on 2026-10-19 with a small Python program; discrete time, no real lock service. Program: brainstorm/system-design-101-vi/experiments/sd-11-031.py (asserts the recorded values).

design_notes_vi: Một khung sáu thẻ cho sáu tình huống và một khung ghi chú kết quả thử khóa hết hạn.
source_deviations: The source gives a definition and six use cases; the lesson keeps them and adds an expiry experiment and a note on fencing tokens that the source does not contain.
The lesson does not claim that a distributed lock is the right tool for each of the six cases.
